identity.title: The Document Is a Tree
identity.description: Every HTML document you'll ever write is a tree of nested elements. This lesson builds the mental model you'll use for the rest of Forge: what nesting actually means, why order and containment matter, and how the browser turns your markup into that structure.

primaryCapability.statement: Model an HTML document as a hierarchical tree of nested parent-child elements.

knows: What a web page roughly is
That web pages contain text and images
likelyMisconceptions: Indentation in HTML is just for readability and has no structural meaning
Elements are placed on a page like objects on a canvas, not contained inside one another

canDo: Read a snippet of HTML and identify which element contains which
Predict how deeply nested a given element is
Construct correctly nested markup for a simple structure

learning.targetMentalModel: An HTML document is not a flat list of tags — it's a tree. Every element (except the root) has exactly one parent, and can have any number of children. Nesting an element inside another means 'this is part of that' — a structural claim, not a visual one.

experience.startingState: The learner has seen HTML before but has never been asked to think about it as a structure with rules.
experience.narrativeContext: A nested snippet is presented as a shape to be understood, not memorized.
experience.primaryInteraction: Predicting containment relationships, then constructing a small nested structure.
experience.expectedOutcome: The learner can look at any nested HTML and correctly say what contains what.

activities.title: Build the Nesting
activities.instruction: Complete the markup so that a <section> contains a <h2> titled "Gear List", and a <ul> containing exactly one <li> with the text "Rope". The <h2> and the <ul> should both be direct children of the <section> — not nested inside each other.

content.starterCode:
<section>
  <!-- add your h2 and ul here -->
</section>

testCases.description: The <h2> is a direct child of <section>
The <ul> is a direct child of <section>, not inside the <h2>

hints.text: You need two separate elements inside <section>, not one inside the other.
A <ul> needs at least one <li> inside it to hold your text.

Gear List

— fill in the text content.

content.prompt: Explain to a teammate who's never seen HTML: what does it mean for one element to be "inside" another? Why isn't that just about how the page looks?
guidelines: Say something about why order/containment is structural, not visual

content.title: What You Can Do Now
takeaways: HTML documents form a tree: every element (except the root) has exactly one parent.
Nesting is a structural claim — "this is part of that" — not a visual effect.
The browser builds this tree from your markup before it renders anything.
nextSteps: Next: configuring what an element does with attributes.

requirements: sufficient contrast for the tree diagram
